tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__claude-artifacts__edit_version
tools.description: Publish a new version of an artifact you own, or of one in your organization that you can edit (some clients refuse any artifact but your own as owner-only), by replacing text in its current document: use it for a small change instead of sending the whole page to publish_version. The server reads the live index.html, applies every edit in order, and publishes the result as one new version; if any edit cannot be applied, nothing is published. Each old_text must occur exactly once in the document as it stands when that edit is applied: include enough surrounding text to make it unique. base_version must name the live version (from get_artifact, read_artifact, list_files or your last publish result); if it is no longer live the call is rejected with a conflict that names the live version: read what you are changing again and retry. To rename the artifact pass title, which also rewrites the document's <title> element; an edit to that element without title is refused, because the server keeps it in step with the artifact's title. Artifacts that contain a live (collaboratively edited) document cannot be edited here. An artifact made from a type is edited only if this server offers list_files, and only with path: one of its own text files, as list_files lists them, never its page or its type's files.

artifact_title.description: The artifact's current title, as get_artifact gives it. Needed when shared_live is 'public'.

base_version.description: The version id these edits apply to: the live version, as get_artifact, read_artifact, list_files or your last publish result returned it.

Required when that value is 'users' (named people or groups), 'org' (the user's whole organization) or 'public' (anyone with the link). Leave it out for a new artifact and when the value is 'owner'. Title, favicon, icon and contract need no echo: omit them on publish_version to keep the values returned here.

tools.name: mcp__claude-artifacts__publish_files
tools.description: Publish an artifact from files on disk: their bytes go from the files to the artifact and do not pass through you. Prefer this to publish_version when the page's files already exist, when there is more than one file or an image, or when the page is large. For each file give `as`, the path it is served at, and `path`, its absolute path on the machine where your own file tools run; leave `uri` out. index.html is required in a new artifact. Limits for one call: 256 files, 20 MiB a file, 64 MiB in all. The client may refuse a file it will not send, such as a secrets file, a link or a path outside the working folder. Omit slug to create an artifact, private to you. To republish, give slug and base_version (from get_artifact, read_artifact or your last publish); title and icon are kept when omitted. A republish changes only the files named and keeps the rest, which stay served: to take a file away, list it in remove. mode "replace" makes the files named the whole artifact and drops the rest. This tool publishes only to an artifact of yours. **Files Claude did not write**: Claude reads the whole file before publishing it, even when the person asks it not to. Publishing distributes the content, and Claude never distributes what it has not seen. A request for privacy is a reason to read before publishing, not an exemption. If Claude cannot read the file, it does not publish it. **Claude never publishes** a page that impersonates a real person or organization, for example by using their name, branding, byline or domain. Claude also never publishes fabricated records, receipts or reviews presented as genuine, forms or flows that collect credentials or payment details under false pretenses, or content that targets a private individual. Claude refuses whether it wrote the page or the person supplied it, and whatever purpose is claimed, such as a prop or a test, when the page would work as the real thing. If publishing is refused, Claude does not suggest other ways to host or share the page.

artifact_title.description: The artifact's current title, as get_artifact gives it. Needed when shared_live is 'public'.

base_version.description: Required when republishing: the version this publish replaces.

contract.description: Optional runtime-contract version. Leave it out to keep the current one.

as.description: The path the file is served at, e.g. index.html or css/site.css. Its extension says what it is served as.

path.description: Give this: the file's absolute path on the machine where your own file tools run.

slug.description: The artifact's slug. Omit to create a new artifact.

tools.name: mcp__claude-artifacts__publish_version
tools.description: Publish an artifact: either create a new artifact — omit slug and give title and content; you become its owner and it starts private to you — or publish a new version of an artifact you own, or of one in your organization that you can edit — give slug and base_version. Some clients may publish only to your own artifacts: there the call is refused as owner-only. Republishing is read-then-send: base_version must name the live version you are replacing (from get_artifact, read_artifact or your last publish result) — if it is no longer live, the publish is rejected with a conflict; re-read and retry from the current state. On success the new version goes live immediately. When republishing, the artifact's stored connectors manifest carries forward unchanged, and so do title, favicon, icon and contract when omitted. Content is capped at 16 MiB.

schema.name: mcp__claude-artifacts__publish_version
schema.description: Publish an artifact: either create a new artifact — omit slug and give title and content; you become its owner and it starts private to you — or publish a new version of an artifact you own, or of one in your organization that you can edit — give slug and base_version. Some clients may publish only to your own artifacts: there the call is refused as owner-only. Republishing is read-then-send: base_version must name the live version you are replacing (from get_artifact, read_artifact or your last publish result) — if it is no longer live, the publish is rejected with a conflict; re-read and retry from the current state. On success the new version goes live immediately. When republishing, the artifact's stored connectors manifest carries forward unchanged, and so do title, favicon, icon and contract when omitted. Content is capped at 16 MiB.

artifact_title.description: The artifact's current title, as get_artifact gives it. Needed when shared_live is 'public'.

base_version.description: Required when slug is given: the version id this publish replaces — echo the version get_artifact or read_artifact returned (or your last publish result's). Rejected with a conflict if it no longer names the live version, so concurrent edits are never silently overwritten. Omit when creating.

content.description: The complete HTML document, at most 16 MiB. Must sniff as text/html — begin it with <!DOCTYPE html>.

contract.description: Optional runtime-contract version (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH). Leave it out to keep the current one. Pass one only when the user asks for a different version, or this server's answer says to. If the publish is rejected because the contract is yanked or out of the supported window, republish with an explicit "0.0.0" to clear the contract — omitting the argument is not a reliable recovery (the server may carry the stored contract forward, repeating the rejection).

deadline.description: Optional, rarely needed: by when pages still open on an OLDER version must have moved to this one — one word: now, 15m, 1h, 24h, 7d, or an ISO-8601 time at most 30 days ahead. Omit it for ordinary edits (open pages then move at their next quiet moment); it cannot be relaxed once published.

favicon.description: Optional legacy emoji marker; omit it.

icon.description: One short, generic word for the artifact's tab icon — a plain signifier of what it is, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map; not a product or brand name. Pass one when creating; omit when republishing to keep the current icon.

# Meshy AI — Workflow Guide

Every create tool returns {task_id, status}, except meshy_creative_lab, which waits and returns the finished model. Wait for it with meshy_get_task_status (task_type is inferred when omitted), then meshy_download_model.
Earlier results: meshy_list_models lists finished 3D models (image-to-3d by default; task_types widens it); meshy_list_tasks lists tasks of any status (default: text-to-3d, image-to-3d, multi-image-to-3d, text-to-image, image-to-image; task_types widens it, so an empty default list does not mean there are no printing, rigging or Creative Lab tasks).

## Rule 1: Cost Confirmation
Before calling ANY tool that costs credits, ask which ai_model to use where there is a choice (prefer an explicit one), present the cost and wait for user confirmation.

| Tool | Credits |
|------|---------|
| meshy_text_to_3d (preview, mesh only) | 20 (meshy-7.1 / latest / meshy-6), 5 (meshy-6-lite, meshy-t2, meshy-t2.5) |
| meshy_image_to_3d / meshy_multi_image_to_3d | table below |
| meshy_text_to_3d_refine / meshy_retexture | 10 (15 with texture_resolution "8k") |
| meshy_remesh / meshy_rig (incl. walking + running) / meshy_uv_unwrap | 5 |
| meshy_animate | 3 per action |
| meshy_text_to_motion | 10 (prime) / 3 (swift) |
| meshy_repair_printability / meshy_process_multicolor / meshy_auto_split | 10 |
| meshy_convert / meshy_resize | 1 |
| meshy_creative_lab | 36; keycap 62; fidget-collapsible 6 |
| meshy_text_to_image / meshy_image_to_image | nano-banana 3, nano-banana-2 6, nano-banana-2-lite 3, nano-banana-2-1 4, nano-banana-pro 9; GPT Image models (gpt-image-2, gpt-image-2-5-flare, gpt-image-2-5-sunburst) 9 text / 12 image |
| analyze printability, balance, usage, animation library, status, list, download | free |

| image / multi-image ai_model | mesh only | + 2K/4K texture | + 8K texture |
|---|---|---|---|
| meshy-7.1 / latest / meshy-6 (and deprecated meshy-7) | 20 | 30 | 35 |
| meshy-6-lite | 5 | 15 | — (2K only) |
| meshy-t2 / meshy-t2.5 (single-image Smart Topology) | 5 | 15 | 20 |

Ultra geometry (geometry_resolution "2k"/"4k") adds 5 on meshy-7.1 / latest. Confirm the 8K and Ultra surcharges explicitly.
Prices match https://docs.meshy.ai/en/api/pricing as of 2026-10-12; point the user there if a number looks off.

## Rule 2: Never Re-create a Task You Are Unsure About
If a create call fails with a timeout, network error or 5xx, the task may still have been created and charged. Check meshy_list_tasks (task_type = that task's type) for it before calling the create tool again. A wait that times out leaves the task running: poll the same task_id again.

## Rule 3: Determine Output Format BEFORE Generating
target_formats is fixed at creation time (3mf only when listed), so ask about the intended use first.

## Rule 4: Identify the Use Case, Then Confirm with User
Determine which scenario below best matches, present a suggested plan to the user, and confirm before executing. When a request spans several scenarios (e.g. A then L), combine their steps and confirm the combined plan.

---

## Scenario A: 3D Printing (white model)
Trigger: user mentions print, slicer, figurine, miniature, statue, physical model — single-color.
Suggested flow:
1. Detect installed slicers (meshy_send_to_slicer, slicer_type:"auto") — present list, save for later
2. Generate an untextured model with target_formats:["obj"]: meshy_text_to_3d (preview), or meshy_image_to_3d with should_texture:false
3. Wait for completion
4. Optionally check printability (meshy_analyze_printability, free). If it reports errors, either repair with model_url = the generation task's OBJ URL (model_urls.obj) so the result stays OBJ — on that route pass printer_type and intended_print_longest_side_mm, since intended_print_height_mm only works with task / GLB input — or repair by the analyze task, then meshy_convert the repaired GLB to obj (1 credit). print_ready only fixes OBJ
5. Download the OBJ (the repair task's, if repaired) with print_ready=true and print_height_mm (local Z-up fix and scaling)

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.
- First navigation for a task is `new_tab(url)`, not `goto_url(url)`. The daemon
  preserves the attached tab across separate CLI invocations, so do not call
  `new_tab()` again in every script.
- Keep one working tab per task/site. Before opening another, inspect
  `current_tab()` and `list_tabs()` and use `switch_tab()` to reuse a matching
  tab. Do not leave duplicate tabs on the same URL or close tabs you did not
  create.
- At task completion, close tabs created for the task that are no longer needed.
  Keep a tab open if the user needs to see it, it is needed for a known follow-up,
  or closing it could discard unsaved work or other important state.
- `new_tab()` and `switch_tab()` attach and move the horse marker without
  changing Chrome's visible tab. Screenshots and normal CDP input work in the
  background. Never call `activate_tab(target)` automatically: it brings Chrome
  to the foreground. Call it only when the user explicitly asks to see or
  visibly switch to that tab. Do not pair `switch_tab()` with `activate_tab()`.
- A local daemon is a connection to the whole Chrome instance, not to one site,
  task, card, or agent. Omit `BU_NAME` and reuse the default daemon for normal
  sequential local work across websites, tabs, screenshots, and Codex turns.
  Do not invent per-job names such as `gmail1375` or `slack1371`: every new
  local daemon opens another browser-level CDP connection and Chrome may show
  another Allow prompt.
- Set `BH_TAB_MARKER=0` before starting the daemon to leave page titles unchanged.
  The horse marker remains enabled by default.
- A timeout or page that pauses while hidden is not permission to foreground
  Chrome. Keep using background CDP operations. For a focus-gated page,
  temporarily call `cdp("Emulation.setFocusEmulationEnabled", enabled=True)`,
  perform and verify the operation, then disable it in a `finally` block. If
  background control still cannot work, report that limitation instead of
  activating the tab. Do not invent a `Runtime.evaluate` scroll replacement or
  a cross-frame JS walker.
- The normal local flow attaches to the running Chrome/Chromium CDP endpoint. No browser ids or local profile selection.

## plugin:desktop-commander:desktop-commander
Desktop Commander provides tools for working with the user's authorized device.
- Filesystem tools handle direct file and directory operations within configured access boundaries.
- Terminal process tools support shell commands, REPLs, and long-running processes. start_process creates a process session; interact_with_process sends input; read_process_output reads later output; force_terminate ends a session.
- Search tools are session-based. start_search creates a search session; get_more_search_results reads its results; stop_search ends it early.
- Absolute paths are generally the most reliable because relative paths depend on the active working directory.
- allowedDirectories and each tool's schema, annotations, and documented constraints define the operational boundaries.

Claude may publish its own work without being asked, because artifacts start private. Claude builds those as files and lets the person decide whether they get a URL. When a finished piece of work is meant for other people or agents, such as a report for a team or the case for a decision the team has yet to make, Claude does not treat it as finished while it exists only in this conversation or in a local file. Claude publishes it and gives the person the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose. Claude publishes it even when the request is phrased as a question, such as "can you write up the plan?". When the request says who else will read or use the work, such as a team, a manager or a reviewer, or where it will be posted or presented, such as a channel or a meeting, Claude publishes it. A recommendation or analysis written up for someone else to act on is finished work for that reader, so Claude publishes it. Call guide before the first publish of a session: it holds the rules a page must meet. This server cannot change who can see an artifact (sharing, publishing to the web, unsharing), delete an artifact or read view counts; say so instead of calling a tool. Here are guidelines for using Supabase tools effectively:

- Apply schema migrations carefully, as changes go directly to the remote project

186	| `PAUSED` | `request_resume` | `RUNNING` | |

211	
212	### Interactions with Other Systems
213	
214	**All 25 other MVP GDDs now exist and passed a registry consistency check on 2026-10-27; the interface notes below remain the kernel's side of each contract, and each consumer's GDD is authoritative for what it registers.** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* The kernel owns the mechanism (registry, dispatcher, phases, subscriber classes); each consumer owns what it registers (block schemas, command types, hooks). Three rules for every consumer, carried into the control manifest: a system that wants state to persist registers a block and never talks to Save/Load directly; a system that wants to change another's state publishes a command or a mutator and never reaches into another's block; a system that wants to *show* state subscribes and reads and never calls into the simulation.

# Design Document Rules

- The 8 GDD sections are: Overview, Player Fantasy, Detailed Rules, Formulas, Edge Cases, Dependencies, Tuning Knobs, Acceptance Criteria
- **How many are required depends on `modes.workflow`** — all 8 at `full`, 5 (+ Formulas when the system **defines numeric rules**: rates, curves, thresholds, costs, damage, drop weights — anything a balance pass would tune) at `standard`, none at `minimal` (the design record there is `design/game-brief.md`). Resolve the tier before flagging a section as missing; see `.claude/docs/workflow-modes.md`
- **The Formulas test is what the system defines, not what it is called.** A system's `Category` in `systems-index.md` is a hint — `Gameplay`, `Economy` and `Progression` almost always qualify — never the test. Do not gate Formulas on a category token: the categories `/map-systems` writes (`Core · Gameplay · Progression · Economy · Persistence · UI · Audio · Narrative · Meta`) do not include `combat` or `AI`, which are example systems *within* `Gameplay`. Every site stating this rule must state the same test.
- **Section-name alias**: The GDD template and `/design-system` author this section as `## Detailed Design`; the design standard calls it **Detailed Rules**. These are the SAME required section — accept either heading and never rewrite one into the other.
- Formulas must include variable definitions, expected value ranges, and example calculations
- Edge cases must explicitly state what happens, not just "handle gracefully"
- Dependencies must be bidirectional — if system A depends on B, B's doc must mention A
- Tuning knobs must specify safe ranges and what gameplay aspect they affect
- Acceptance criteria must be testable — a QA tester must be able to verify pass/fail
- No hand-waving: "the system should feel good" is not a valid specification
- Balance values must link to their source formula or rationale
- Design documents MUST be written incrementally: create skeleton first, then fill
  each section one at a time with user approval between sections. Write each
  approved section to the file immediately to persist decisions and manage context

# Design Directory

When authoring or editing files in this directory, follow these standards.

## GDD Files (`design/gdd/`)

The 8 GDD sections, in order:
1. Overview — one-paragraph summary
2. Player Fantasy — intended feeling and experience
3. Detailed Rules — unambiguous mechanics
4. Formulas — all math defined with variables
5. Edge Cases — unusual situations handled
6. Dependencies — other systems listed
7. Tuning Knobs — configurable values identified
8. Acceptance Criteria — testable success conditions

**How many are REQUIRED depends on `modes.workflow`** — all 8 at `full`; 5 at
`standard` (Overview, Detailed Rules, Edge Cases, Dependencies, Acceptance
Criteria, plus Formulas when the system has math); none at `minimal`, where
`design/game-brief.md` is the design record instead of a GDD. Resolve the tier
before flagging a section as missing — see `.claude/docs/workflow-modes.md`.

> **Three other places already encode the tier rule** —
> `.claude/docs/coding-standards.md`, `.claude/rules/design-docs.md` and
> `.claude/hooks/validate-commit.sh`. This file is the copy a session working in
> `design/` reads first, so it must agree with them: demanding all 8 at
> `minimal` warns a jam project about six sections its own configuration says it
> does not need, which trains the user to ignore the warning.

**Section-name alias:** the GDD template and `/design-system` author section 3
as `## Detailed Design`; the standard calls it **Detailed Rules**. Same required
section — accept either heading, never rewrite one into the other.

**File naming:** `[system-slug].md` (e.g. `movement-system.md`, `combat-system.md`)

**Systems index:** `design/gdd/systems-index.md` — update when adding a new GDD.

**Design order:** Foundation → Core → Feature → Presentation → Polish

**Validation:** Run `/design-review [path]` after authoring any GDD.
Run `/review-all-gdds` after completing a set of related GDDs.

## Quick Specs (`design/quick-specs/`)

Lightweight specs for tuning changes, minor mechanics, or balance adjustments.
Use `/quick-design` to author.

## UX Specs (`design/ux/`)

- Per-screen specs: `design/ux/[screen-name].md`
- HUD design: `design/ux/hud.md`
- Interaction pattern library: `design/ux/interaction-patterns.md`
- Accessibility requirements: `design/accessibility-requirements.md`

Use `/ux-design` to author. Validate with `/ux-review` before passing to `/team-ui`.

> **Accessibility requirements sit OUTSIDE `design/ux/` on purpose.** They are a
> project-wide standard the per-screen specs consult, not a spec for one screen.
> `.claude/docs/workflow-catalog.yaml`, the Pre-Production, Production and Polish
> gates, and `/architecture-review` all check `design/accessibility-requirements.md`
> at that exact path. Do not "tidy" it under `design/ux/` — every one of those
> checks would stop matching, and the Technical Setup → Pre-Production gate would
> become unpassable. `/ux-design` states the same rule at its `accessibility` mode.

# Design Directory

When authoring or editing files in this directory, follow these standards.

## GDD Files (`design/gdd/`)

The 8 GDD sections, in order:
1. Overview — one-paragraph summary
2. Player Fantasy — intended feeling and experience
3. Detailed Rules — unambiguous mechanics
4. Formulas — all math defined with variables
5. Edge Cases — unusual situations handled
6. Dependencies — other systems listed
7. Tuning Knobs — configurable values identified
8. Acceptance Criteria — testable success conditions

**How many are REQUIRED depends on `modes.workflow`** — all 8 at `full`; 5 at
`standard` (Overview, Detailed Rules, Edge Cases, Dependencies, Acceptance
Criteria, plus Formulas when the system has math); none at `minimal`, where
`design/game-brief.md` is the design record instead of a GDD. Resolve the tier
before flagging a section as missing — see `.claude/docs/workflow-modes.md`.

> **Three other places already encode the tier rule** —
> `.claude/docs/coding-standards.md`, `.claude/rules/design-docs.md` and
> `.claude/hooks/validate-commit.sh`. This file is the copy a session working in
> `design/` reads first, so it must agree with them: demanding all 8 at
> `minimal` warns a jam project about six sections its own configuration says it
> does not need, which trains the user to ignore the warning.

**Section-name alias:** the GDD template and `/design-system` author section 3
as `## Detailed Design`; the standard calls it **Detailed Rules**. Same required
section — accept either heading, never rewrite one into the other.

**File naming:** `[system-slug].md` (e.g. `movement-system.md`, `combat-system.md`)

**Systems index:** `design/gdd/systems-index.md` — update when adding a new GDD.

**Design order:** Foundation → Core → Feature → Presentation → Polish

**Validation:** Run `/design-review [path]` after authoring any GDD.
Run `/review-all-gdds` after completing a set of related GDDs.

## Quick Specs (`design/quick-specs/`)

Lightweight specs for tuning changes, minor mechanics, or balance adjustments.
Use `/quick-design` to author.

## UX Specs (`design/ux/`)

- Per-screen specs: `design/ux/[screen-name].md`
- HUD design: `design/ux/hud.md`
- Interaction pattern library: `design/ux/interaction-patterns.md`
- Accessibility requirements: `design/accessibility-requirements.md`

Use `/ux-design` to author. Validate with `/ux-review` before passing to `/team-ui`.

> **Accessibility requirements sit OUTSIDE `design/ux/` on purpose.** They are a
> project-wide standard the per-screen specs consult, not a spec for one screen.
> `.claude/docs/workflow-catalog.yaml`, the Pre-Production, Production and Polish
> gates, and `/architecture-review` all check `design/accessibility-requirements.md`
> at that exact path. Do not "tidy" it under `design/ux/` — every one of those
> checks would stop matching, and the Technical Setup → Pre-Production gate would
> become unpassable. `/ux-design` states the same rule at its `accessibility` mode.

110	**CR-6. Registration at boot, then frozen.** Block, command-type, hook, diagnostics-channel and binding-source registration are legal only in `BOOTING` *(Amended 2026-10-27 — consistency pass, routed from debug-overlay-true-values (E-DO-38))* (a block may declare one optional `binding_source` callable, CR-7; one registered after `BOOTING` is refused like every other registration *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)*); after `BOOTING → LOADING` the registries are immutable until shutdown. Registration is an explicit declaration by the composition root, not discovery via the scene tree. Duplicate IDs, unknown types, missing owners and hook cycles fail boot loudly in every build. A command type registered without `allowed_origins`, `actor_binding`, `coalesce` or `max_age_ticks` (**no silent defaults**: an omitted `actor_binding` must never mean 'no ownership check'), a type with `actor_binding = OWNED_BY_ISSUER` but no `actor_source`, one whose `actor_source` names a block that registered no `binding_source`, and a `NONE` type that declares an `actor_source` (each fails boot with `ACTOR_SOURCE_INVALID`, naming the type) *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)*, a block registered without `class`, `gameplay`, `repl_hint` or `persist`, a type whose `writes_blocks` names an unregistered block, and an `allowed_when_paused` type whose `writes_blocks` names any `gameplay = true` block likewise fail boot (`BOOTING → FAULTED`) naming the registration. *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* A type with `coalesce ≠ NONE` that allows both origins fails boot (`COALESCE_DUAL_ORIGIN`), because the supersession key carries no origin (D.8); and the joint memory assertion of Section G constraint 8 is checked here *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)*.
111	
112	**CR-7. Authority model (behaviour).** The host is the sole authority: only a `HOST` kernel ticks and applies; a `MIRROR` never applies. Each command type's owner declares `allowed_origins ⊆ {PLAYER, SYSTEM}` and `actor_binding ∈ {NONE, OWNED_BY_ISSUER}` — both mandatory (CR-6) — and `allowed_origins` is checked at admission, with a P2 re-check as defence in depth. *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* A type with `actor_binding = OWNED_BY_ISSUER` also declares **`actor_source`**: the `block_id` of the registered binding source whose ID space its `actor` belongs to (`body.state` for every avatar-acting type, `emitter.state` for `toggle_beam`). The P2 authority check passes iff `(actor_source(type), actor) ∈ half_b[PlayerId(issuer_peer)]`. So an actor and a beam with the same number can never stand in for each other. *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)* `SYSTEM` commands never arrive from a network; remote ingress always stamps `PLAYER`. The kernel holds a **binding table** — `peer_id → PlayerId` and `PlayerId → {(source block_id, entity_id)}` — as identity data, not domain state; the table has two halves with different lifetimes *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix; Resolved 2026-10-28 — delegated ruling G6 (user delegated all remaining calls): the kernel owns the rebuild; closes Body Open Question 30)*. **(a) `peer_id → PlayerId`** is session state: it is mutated only through a host-only API called by the session owner (a boot step in MVP: `HOST_PEER_ID` 1 → PlayerId 1; Co-op Session in VS-B), and a restore, a death restart or a new game never touches it and never resets any issuer's `seq` or `last_seq`. **(b) `PlayerId → {(source block_id, entity_id)}`** *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)* is derived from saved state and is never saved: **the kernel rebuilds it itself as the last step of every pass through `LOADING`** (`request_restore` and `request_new_game` alike), after the last `post_restore()` and the K-4 hash check and before the `LOADING → RUNNING` transition. The rebuild clears half (b) entirely, then calls each registered **binding source** (CR-6, CR-8) in ascending `block_id` order — with `ctx`, as a pure read of its owner's block, under no `WriteScope`, ending `return ctx.complete()` — which delivers `[(player_id, entity_id)]` in ascending order through `ctx.put`, and binds every pair under the source's own `block_id`: each delivered `(player_id, entity_id)` is stored as `player_id → (source_block_id, entity_id)`. Entity IDs are block-local (CR-8: each owner allocates from its own counter and the kernel allocates none), so the key always carries the source. Equal numbers from two sources (Body actor 1 and Emitter beam 1) are two different keys and never conflict. A key `(source_block_id, entity_id)` delivered for two different PlayerIds, or the same triple `(player_id, source_block_id, entity_id)` delivered twice, is `BINDING_REBUILD_CONFLICT`. A source that reports `ctx.fault` or returns without the sentinel is that source's fault. Either one takes `LOADING → FAULTED` naming the source. The checks compare keys only within one source. *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix; registry request: `kernel_binding_table` `half_b`, `errors`, `actor_source`, `referenced_by`)* Because `LOADING` is atomic within one boundary service, the rebuild is not a P6 control-plane request and no command can interleave with it; the P6 rule (Section E) governs session-owner changes to half (a) only. At MVP no binding source's pairs change during `RUNNING`, so no `RUNNING` tick sees an empty or stale half (b); a runtime seat or beam reassignment (VS-B) is a session-owner request honoured at P6 (Open Question 4, the co-op ADR). MVP binding sources: Body's `seat_bindings()` (its `SEAT` rows → `(seat, actor_id)`) and the Emitter's `beam_bindings()` (`(player_id, beam_id)`). Single-player: PlayerId 1 → {(`body.state`, avatar actor_id), (`emitter.state`, beam_id)}. Both numbers may be 1 (two independent counters), and the result is valid. *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix. Resolved 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix (G6): keyed by source rather than by namespace-tagged IDs, so Body's and the Emitter's persisted ID formats stay unchanged (G1).)* *(Alternative: Player Controller owns the binding as a block — rejected because the kernel could then not authority-check without calling a domain system. → ADR.)* **Single-player is not a special case**: local input is `PLAYER`-origin peer 1 (registry: `HOST_PEER_ID` = 1) acting on an entity peer 1 is bound to; the authority stage runs on every command from day one, so TD-FEASIBILITY's "authority discipline lapsing" risk is structural, not disciplinary. The kernel checks *who*; owners validate *whether the world allows it*; the kernel encodes no game rules. For friendly harm the kernel checks only issuer→actor ownership; the "attacker below the sanity threshold" gate is Interaction's `validate` calling Sanity's query on the actor's authoritative sanity level (a `SIM` block), never on anyone's perception.

I'm also checking KRN-STATE-02's "fresh process ran request_new_game at first boot" scenario is now valid, and noting that KRN-STATE-01's enumeration of state/trigger pairs will need the BOOTING split accounted for.

I need to update KRN-STATE-01 to add BOOTING→LOADING on request_new_game/request_restore plus DEFERRED entries for SAVING/LOADING, and adjust the tested-pair count formula to include deferred pairs. I'm also working through how a fixture could even drive a request "during" atomic LOADING — likely via a callback like post_restore calling request_pause — and distinguishing that from a same-boundary request_pause arriving alongside request_restore, both of which fall under DEFERRED; I'm also rechecking that L170's SAVING rule aligns with this treatment.

Restore requests during SAVING get queued per L198, which I'm naming DEFERRED, and I'm checking request_snapshot during SAVING: the kernel defers it (producing a second capture after the current one completes) while Save/Load simply chooses not to issue a second snapshot, so the two layers are consistent. Shutdown requests during LOADING/SAVING are also DEFERRED, served right after the atomic step, whereas shutdown during BOOTING is served normally since BOOTING isn't atomic. I'm noting DEFERRED as an outcome of a control-plane request rather than a command state, to be documented in the transitions table as producing a diagnostics record of (state, trigger, DEFERRED).

Diagnostics should log a distinct `deferred` entry, separate from the invalid-transition entry, and after deferral the request gets re-evaluated against whatever state the atomic step lands in — SAVING resolves to the prior state or FAULTED, LOADING resolves to RUNNING or FAULTED — with any now-invalid request producing an ordinary invalid-transition entry instead. I'm also working through a trickier edge case: a request_restore deferred during LOADING needs to be served at the boundary immediately following LOADING's completion, consistent with CR-15's rule that same-boundary requests are served in arrival order.

I'm settling on consistent phrasing — "served at the boundary that follows the atomic step (next boundary service, CR-15)" — matching how L991 describes restore-after-SAVING. For the DOCK subject `console_ready` additionally requires the dock to be HOME's. Within the DOCK subject the rows are selected by one more pure read published here, `berthed_present()` (true iff a derelict is berthed, from the persisted berth fields): `unberth` (priority 1, eligible iff `berthed_present`) and `berth` (priority 2, eligible iff not `berthed_present`), so Interaction's `select_verb` (IA-5) stays a function of (class, tool, eligible) and the plate shows `unberth` while a record is berthed (CT-10 R5). A DOCK press away from HOME cannot occur (no DOCK subject exists at a derelict dock, CT-10 R1b); through a test double it returns `NOT_DOCKED_HERE`. A POD press at HOME with a derelict berthed and no valid pick is routed to this system and returns `BERTH_PENDING` (WM-9, CT-10 R6). From a derelict the press carries HOME implicitly. *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)* The prompt belongs to Interaction; no Web Map & Transit HUD element exists (guard rail 1). The Chart Table's confirm gesture may issue a resume then the console press; that is the Chart Table's design call (Chart Table designed). **Gap carried to Authoring/Layout:** Derelict Authoring authors the docked-podcraft prop (DA-6, kit gap K-3) but no pod-console declaration; the console is this GDD's requirement on the prop's `subject_anchors` entry (ASK-L3 to Authoring and Layout, OPEN, OQ-DA-39; ASK-I1 to Interaction, accepted). *Cites.* IA:131 (`pod_hop`, "Web Map's"), IA-37; DA-6; KRN CR-16; CT-10 R1b, R6; ASK-CT-13, ASK-CT-14 (ANSWERED 2026-10-28: Interaction draws the text-free pick echo, IA-40; this system holds no pick). *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)* *Pillar.* P1 (the press is the commitment; the chart is a human instrument). *Decided.* R15.

It is therefore **not** a fourth `act_gate` exception and Interaction changes nothing. (1) **On iff the prop is present (WM-33)** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review, delegated ruling G1)*: each dock room's one DOCK_STATUS glow record is created OFF at `init_world` (Emitter E1) and this system switches it with Emitter's E10 `set_dock_status(section_id, on)` **inside the apply that writes `pod_at`**: ON for the home dock in `init_world` step 7, OFF for the origin dock in the `pod_hop` departure apply (WM-10), ON for the target dock in `pod_settle` (WM-14; this includes the settle that ends a T5 reversed leg, WM-15), and **no call at `berth` or `unberth`** (the pod does not move, `pod_at` is unwritten, and the verbs run only at HOME where the home glow is already ON). The cull is presentation only (ASK-PIPE, OQ-WM-47) and is a derived input of D.6; a zoom lock is not used because it would contradict the zoom in/out decision. *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)* **The cull is specified per pixel, with a fade band, so nothing pops.** It is a mask on the exterior layer (the wreck silhouette, the residual-lamp point with its halo, and the departure hull), evaluated per pixel on the distance `r` from the pod's centre in base px, not per object: a pixel is fully drawn for `r <= EXTERIOR_CULL_RADIUS_PX - EXTERIOR_CULL_FADE_PX`, fully culled for `r >= EXTERIOR_CULL_RADIUS_PX`, and in between it is drawn at one of four **ordered-dither coverage steps** (a 4x4 Bayer mask at 25, 50, 75 and 100 %, so the pixel grid and the palette are kept; there is no alpha blend and no scale change). 76:**CR-3. Step hooks and ordering.** Hooks register `(hook_id, owner, divisor, offset, after: [hook_id | {hook_id, tolerates_stale}])`. The kernel resolves a total order by topological sort of `after`; ties break by registration order, then `hook_id`. A cycle or unknown `hook_id` fails boot (CR-6). Sim-to-sim data flow within a tick is "reader declares `after` writer" (Suit vitals `after: graph.propagate.atmo` — the Graph registers three chained hooks, see its LS-1 *(Amended 2026-10-26 — consistency check, routed from the Life-Support Graph GDD)*). The order is data: testable, and printable by the Debug Overlay. An `after` edge between two hooks that never run in the same tick (Section E) must carry `tolerates_stale: true` if the reader accepts data up to a divisor old; boot warns only for **undeclared** mismatches, so the real boot (`horror.step` divisor 5 after `attention.step` di

96:**CR-5. Command lifecycle and the exactly-one-result guarantee.** Every command reaches exactly one terminal state and emits exactly one result record (identified by `result_id`; delivered to its issuer unless it is `SYSTEM`-origin, see Result identity and delivery below). Stages: *Issued* → *Admission* (kernel state accepts commands; type registered; **origin allowed for the type — known at admission, so rejected there**; queue not full; `seq` not a duplicate — gaps are accepted and counted, not rejected; issuer rate limit; payload plain) → *Queued* → *Authority check* in P2 (origin re-checked as a defence in depth; if the type declares `actor_binding = OWNED_BY_ISSUER`, the binding table says the issuer controls the key `(actor_source, actor)` *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)*; age ≤ the type's `max_age_ticks`) → *Validate* (owner's side-effect-free `validate(cm

78	**CR-4. Command anatomy, origin and intents.** A command is plain serializable data:
79	
80	| Field | Meaning |
81	|-------|---------|
82	| `type` | Registered command type ID, owned by a domain system |
83	| `issuer_peer` | Stamped by the kernel's ingress — never taken from the payload |
84	| `origin` | `PLAYER` or `SYSTEM`, stamped by ingress |
85	| `actor` | The entity the command acts as: an opaque ID in the ID space of the type's declared `actor_source` block (CR-7; IDs are block-local, CR-8, so one number can name different entities in two blocks), or none *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)* |
86	| `seq` | Monotonically increasing integer per `(issuer_peer, origin)` — the host's `PLAYER` and `SYSTEM` streams are separate spaces *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*. **Stamped by the kernel at ISSUED, never chosen by a local caller**: every local `INPUT_SURFACE` handle and `submit_system()` receives the next value of the one kernel-held counter for its `(issuer_peer, origin)`, so any number of surfaces sharing the `(1, PLAYER)` space can never collide; the counter advances on every submit, including one rejected at admission, so locally stamped values are dense (1, 2, 3 …) and `DUPLICATE_SEQ` and gap counting apply only to a `seq` supplied by the **test ingress or a remote ingress** (the only two callers that may supply one) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review, delegated ruling R2)* |
87	| `correlation` | Optional opaque `int` the submitting caller attaches (default 0 = none); the kernel never interprets it and echoes it unchanged in the command's result record and in any rejection event, so a caller (the Player Controller's pre-play tokens, a menu) matches a result to the act that caused it without learning or choosing `seq`. Kernel metadata like `submission_id`, never payload-borne; not part of `canonical_bytes` or any hash. Not unique: two submits may carry the same `correlation` *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review, delegated ruling R2)* |
88	| `payload` | Plain data only, per the recursive whitelist below; no object references, node paths or callables; `var_to_bytes(payload, false).size()` ≤ `MAX_PAYLOAD` |
89	| `queued_tick` | Stamped on enqueue |
90	| `submission_id` | Kernel metadata, never payload-borne: a kernel-unique counter stamped at ISSUED, before admission, so even a rejected submit has one; it is the `result_id` of the command's result (CR-5) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* |
91	
92	*Discrete commands vs continuous intents.* If the sim must log, validate, save or replay it, it is a command (examples; each type's owner GDD is authoritative: Controller `set_move_intent`, `set_aim`, `toggle_beam`; Interaction `begin_cut` (module salvage, V8), `begin_patch`, `cancel_channel`, `pickup`, `drop`, `set_switch`, `field_check`; Modular Ship Assembly `begin_weld` (declared by Interaction, registered by Assembly), `begin_seam_cut`, `install_module` and the `SYSTEM`-only completions `weld` / `seam_cut` (registry: `assembly_commands`; there is no `remove_module` — it is reserved and unregistered, and V8 salvage is the only removal); Suit `equip_tool` (its only type); Web Map & Transit `pod_hop`, `berth`, `unberth` and the `SYSTEM`-only `pod_arrive`, `pod_settle`, `berth_step`, `web_reconcile` (registry: `web_commands`). `interact` is an input action, not a command type, and `use_item` has no owner and is not a command *(Amended 2026-10-27 — consistency pass, routed from interaction-system, suit-and-equipment, modular-ship-assembly and web-map-and-transit)*). What the stick is doing *right now* is an intent: intents are commands too, but a type may declare `coalesce = LATEST_PER_ACTOR_PER_TICK` — coalescing happens at admission over the unfrozen queue, keyed `(type, actor, issuer_peer)`, the older command becoming `Superseded` — and the input adapter sends one only when the quantised value changes — a few per second, never one per tick. Edge-triggered inputs (press, release, confirm) must declare `coalesce = NONE` or taps are lost. Movement integration runs inside the sim: Body's `body.integrate` hook (divisor 1, P3) reads the current intent and integrates ship-local kinematics (CR-13), so a move intent takes effect one tick after it is submitted, like every command; there is no physics-side integration at MVP, and position ownership is settled (Body owns it; the Controller owns intent and facing) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*. Under `STRICT_DEBUG` every command is round-tripped through serialization before dispatch, even locally; one that cannot survive is a violation (CR-19). **Submit is fire-and-forget and never calls back**: `submit()` returns nothing and invokes no callback, handler or subscriber, so it is safe to call from any handler, hook or result handler; its only outcome is one result record appended to the kernel's result buffer (CR-5), delivered at the next flush and identified by `result_id` — a remote issuer could never get a synchronous answer, so the local one doesn't either *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*. `submit()` takes the optional `correlation` and returns nothing, not even a receipt: the caller learns the outcome only from the result record, which carries its `correlation` back, so "fire-and-forget" is literally true and `seq` stays the kernel's. The API shape is `submit(type, payload, actor = none, correlation = 0)` on an `INPUT_SURFACE` handle and `submit_system(type, payload, dedupe_key = none)` for hooks (a hook needs no correlation: it never receives a result) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review, delegated ruling R2)*.
93	
94	**Payload whitelist** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*. 'Plain' is a recursive `Variant.Type` whitelist checked at admission: `NIL`, `BOOL`, `INT`, `FLOAT` (finite only — `NaN` and `±inf` are `MALFORMED`; the same finite check applies to **each component of a `VECTOR2` and each element of `PackedFloat32Array`, `PackedFloat64Array` and `PackedVector2Array`**, which the walk visits in O(n) bounded by `MAX_PAYLOAD` *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)*), `STRING`, `STRING_NAME`, `VECTOR2`, `VECTOR2I`, the `Packed{Byte,Int32,Int64,Float32,Float64,String,Vector2}Array` types, and `ARRAY`/`DICTIONARY` of the same, to a depth cap `PAYLOAD_MAX_DEPTH` = 8 (which also rejects a self-containing container). Dictionary keys must be `INT`, `STRING` or `STRING_NAME` and **all keys of one dictionary must share one type** (mixed keys have no canonical order, D.12). Anything else — an `Object`, `NodePath`, `Callable`, `Signal`, `RID`, a non-whitelisted `Variant.Type`, a non-finite float, a depth-9 nesting, mixed dictionary keys — is `MALFORMED`; the size bound is measured as `var_to_bytes(payload, false).size()` after the walk passes. Immediate *acknowledgement* (a tool sound, a hand animation, a linear progress bar starting) is presentation's job and happens in the same frame; the sim confirms on the next tick. The latency bounds are stated once, in Game Feel and D.4.

content.content:
*Intents vs commands (CR-4).* Two types are **intents**, `coalesce = LATEST_PER_ACTOR_PER_TICK`, `max_age_ticks = 30`: **`set_move_intent {octant: 0..7 | 8 = NONE, run: bool}`** and **`set_aim {aim_angle: int, live: bool}`** in **1/4096-turn units** (`live` is `aim_live`: it travels with the angle because facing rules 4–6 branch on it in the sim). Both intents carry `actor_binding = OWNED_BY_ISSUER` with `actor_source = body.state` (the avatar's Body `actor_id`, kernel CR-7), like commands. Everything else is a **command**: `coalesce = NONE`, `max_age_ticks = 120`, `actor_binding = OWNED_BY_ISSUER`, `actor_source` as its owner declares (`body.state` for every avatar-acting verb; `emitter.state` for `toggle_beam`, whose `actor` is the seat's beam id) *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)*. The Adapter sends `set_move_intent` **only on change** of octant or `run`, with the stick quantised to 8 octants under `MOVE_DEADZONE` = 0.25 and `OCTANT_HYSTERESIS_DEG` = 5°. In one frame it submits `set_move_intent` **before** any command (submission order is the P2 apply order — the kernel stamps `seq` internally per (peer, source) from it, and callers never choose it, delegated ruling R2 — so a stop and a `begin_*` in the same frame apply in that order, PC-7). It sends `set_aim` when the quantised value differs from `last_acked` by **≥ 1/128 turn (2.8°)**, **or** the aim source changed (mouse ↔ stick ↔ keys), **or** `live` changed, **or** a settle condition holds (inside 

114:erb; `interact` is an input action.** Each verb is its own command type with its own `validate`, reason subset, `max_age_ticks` 120 (`MAX_AGE_TICKS_ACTION`; `STALE` is unreachable from local ingress), `coalesce NONE` (edge-triggered), `actor_binding OWNED_BY_ISSUER` with `actor_source body.state` (the acting avatar's Body `actor_id`; kernel CR-7 keys the authority check `(body.state, actor)`) *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix: kernel CR-6 / CR-7 make `actor_source` mandatory on every `OWNED_BY_ISSUER` typ
475:ned) | the submit → admission → authority → `validate` → `apply` pipeline; tick `T`; `ticks_for_seconds`; admission reasons; the `WriteScope` token; hook and block registries | the command types of IA-3 (primitive payloads, `coalesce NONE`, `OWNED_BY_ISSUER` with `actor_source body.state` *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)*); result events carrying reasons, never strings; block `interaction.state` and hook `interaction.step`; no RNG | Kernel: CR-3 hook tuple, CR-4 command anatomy, CR-5 result even
